config.title: Berlin Ghost Stations: FAQ
config.subtitle: Which 15 underground stations closed, why Bornholmer Straße makes 16 in all, and what you can visit today.

items.q: What were the Berlin ghost stations?
items.a: They were stations closed to passengers after the Berlin Wall went up on 13 August 1961, while trains continued to pass through. This guide counts 15 underground stations: five on the U6, six on the U8 and four in the north–south S-Bahn tunnel. Adding above-ground Bornholmer Straße gives 16 closed stations in all. The routes connected parts of West Berlin through East Berlin territory. Trains continued operating, while the closed entrances and platforms were secured and guarded.

items.q: Which Berlin stations were ghost stations?
items.a: On the U6: Schwartzkopffstraße, Naturkundemuseum, Oranienburger Tor, Französische Straße and Stadtmitte. On the U8: Bernauer Straße, Rosenthaler Platz, Weinmeisterstraße, Alexanderplatz, Jannowitzbrücke and Heinrich-Heine-Straße. In the north–south S-Bahn tunnel: Nordbahnhof, Oranienburger Straße, Brandenburger Tor and Potsdamer Platz. These are 15 underground stations. Bornholmer Straße was above ground and makes 16 in all. At Stadtmitte, only the U6 platform closed; the U2 platform remained open. Friedrichstraße stayed open and is outside this closed-station count.

items.q: Can you still visit the Berlin ghost stations today?
items.a: Fifteen of the sixteen are working stations today. Französische Straße is closed again. The others have been renovated and returned to service. Start at Nordbahnhof, where a free permanent exhibition on the mezzanine explains the closed stations and underground border. It needs no ticket and can be seen during normal S-Bahn operating hours. Nordbahnhof remains a working station, with the exhibition inside it.

Friedrichstraße remained a transfer point between western U-Bahn and S-Bahn services. Passengers could change trains without border checks inside a separate transfer area. Leaving that area to enter East Berlin required border controls. The station was also a border crossing, whose former departure hall is the Tränenpalast. It is one interchange, even though the map shows it on both the U6 and S-Bahn lines.

items.q: When did the Berlin ghost stations reopen?
items.a: They reopened in stages. Jannowitzbrücke on the U8 was first on 11 November 1989. Rosenthaler Platz followed on 22 December 1989 and Bernauer Straße partially reopened on 12 April 1990. The remaining U6 and U8 stations reopened on 1 July 1990. Oranienburger Straße followed on 2 July 1990, and Nordbahnhof and Unter den Linden, today Brandenburger Tor, on 1 September 1990. Potsdamer Platz was last on 1 March 1992, after renovation of the north–south S-Bahn tunnel.

items.q: Is any Berlin ghost station still closed?
items.a: Yes, but not for Cold War reasons. Französische Straße on the U6 closed permanently on 3 December 2020. The new Unter den Linden station opened the following day one stop up the line as the interchange between the U5 and U6, and Französische Straße was no longer needed. If you go looking for it, get off at Unter den Linden instead.

Bornholmer Straße was a closed above-ground S-Bahn station beneath the Bösebrücke, which carried a border crossing between Prenzlauer Berg and Wedding. On 9 November 1989, selective departures began there at around 21:20. The crossing opened generally at around 23:30. Those are different stages of the same evening, rather than one opening time.

items.q: What is the best way to see this history in one morning?
items.a: Take the S-Bahn to Nordbahnhof, spend about twenty minutes at the free ghost stations exhibition on the mezzanine, then walk straight up onto Bernauer Straße for the Berlin Wall Memorial. You go from how the tunnels were sealed to how the surface was sealed in about ninety seconds of walking, and the whole thing costs nothing beyond your transport ticket.
